Strip hedge. Why serious producers hedge the curve, not a single month.

A producer with steady production over the next 12 months has a choice. Hedge the whole year as a strip (equal contract size in each forward month). Or hedge a single representative month (December crude, for example). Both achieve "I am hedged on next year's production." Only one actually matches the cash flow exposure.

The 5 things to understand about strip hedging in commodity.

1. What a strip is
A simultaneous position across multiple consecutive maturities, usually equal size in each, that mirrors the production or consumption profile over a defined period. A 12-month crude strip is long or short equal contract amounts in each of the next 12 monthly contracts. The strip price is the average of those 12 forward prices.

2. Why strip matches cash flow
A producer pumping equal barrels each month sells at the price prevailing that month. The relevant hedging price is therefore the average of those 12 prices, not December's price. A strip locks in that average. A single-month hedge locks in one point of that average and leaves the other 11 floating.

3. Capital efficiency
Margin on a strip is often calculated on the spread risk between months, not on the gross outright exposure of all 12 months. Exchanges recognize the spread nature. A 12-month strip on crude requires meaningfully less initial margin than 12 independent outright positions. This matters for producers who size hedges against working capital.

4. The execution mistake
The most common mistake: hedging the whole 12-month strip on a single day, in a single execution window, with no consideration for liquidity in deferred months. Front-month liquidity is deep. Back-month liquidity is thin. Stuffing size into back months on a single day creates impact cost that destroys the supposed precision of the strip hedge. Better practice: stage the execution, work the back months separately.

5. Rolling and rebalancing
A 12-month strip becomes an 11-month strip as time passes. Eventually each month expires. The producer either lets the hedge run off (and sells unhedged production at expiry) or rolls into a new 12-month strip continuously. Roll mechanics, basis between expiry and new contract, and timing all introduce additional risk. Most serious hedging programs roll quarterly or monthly, not at expiry, to smooth out single-day roll risk.

A strip hedge matches the actual exposure profile of production or consumption. A single-month hedge is a directional bet on one specific maturity dressed up as risk management. Any producer or consumer with continuous flow needs to think in strips, not in single contracts.

For anyone running a hedging program: do you strip-hedge or single-month, and how do you stage execution?

For long term production supported by sales contracts, the most risk neutral strategy I’ve seen is to take a strip hedge on purchases and sales and include a volume commitment from the customer to prevent forecast error impacting PnL. Leave some capacity for spot sales of production incase of significant production impacts. If the forward curve is not in your favor you build the additional margin in adder to the underlying index. You unwind your hedges as the contact mature, and inventory moves out. 

For long term production not supported by sales contracts, you put on a hedge as inventory prices into stock, and unwind it as it prices out. This way you can always sell spot. There are other strategies behind this (rolling, pricing further on futures curve to flip the position depending on forward curve shape-to name a few.), but this is the basic idea.

Then the traders take you book, give you the PnL and make money off the back of your trading program (lol).

Theron M. Very well said, Theron. This is exactly where hedge design becomes a commercial problem, not just a derivatives problem.
For long-term contracted production, the cleanest hedge often starts with the sales contract itself: indexed pricing, volume commitment, tolerance bands and a clear mechanism for forecast error. The derivative then follows the commercial exposure instead of trying to solve a poorly defined risk.
For uncontracted production or inventory, I agree with your point: hedge as the inventory prices into stock and unwind as it prices out. That keeps the hedge tied to the physical position and preserves the ability to sell spot.
And yes, once the program is clean enough, the trading desk will always find a way to extract some value from the book.

Calum Austin Very good point, Calum. I fully agree.
A strip hedge is often the cleaner structure from a risk management perspective, because it matches the production profile more closely.
But in practice, liquidity, bid/ask, tenor depth and execution size can make the clean hedge expensive or difficult to execute.
That is where producers face the real trade-off: accept roll risk with a stack-and-roll strategy, or use a more liquid but less correlated instrument and take more basis risk.
The optimal hedge is not always the most theoretically precise one. It is the one the company can actually execute, fund and manage through the cycle.
